summary: Describes a syntax for embedding S-HTTP negotiation parameters in HTML documents so that a web page can tell a browser how to set up secure exchanges. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2659 defines HTML additions that associate S-HTTP negotiation information with links and form submissions. The additions can identify a recipient, provide a nonce, list cryptographic options, and include certificate data.

questions: how does html carry s-http settings
what are the certs and cryptopts elements
subtitle: HTML attributes can carry S-HTTP negotiation details for a link.

tldr.problem: S-HTTP negotiation settings need a way to be associated with HTML links and form submissions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the DN, NONCE, and CRYPTOPTS anchor attributes, plus CERTS and CRYPTOPTS elements for certificate data and named cryptographic options.
tldr.outcome: The Experimental RFC describes a syntax for placing S-HTTP negotiation parameters in HTML documents.

today: RFC 2659 defines Experimental HTML syntax for S-HTTP negotiation information. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or replaces it.

sections.title: Binding S-HTTP Settings to HTML
sections.content:
S-HTTP uses negotiation headers to express the receiver's preferences for cryptographic protections. RFC 2659 defines a syntax for binding those settings to HTML anchors and form submissions.

The RFC introduces three attributes: DN gives the distinguished name of the principal for whom the request should be encrypted; NONCE supplies a string for the SHTTP-Nonce header; and CRYPTOPTS carries cryptographic option information defined by S-HTTP.
sections.plainLanguage: HTML links and form submissions can carry S-HTTP settings. The settings can name the intended recipient, provide a nonce, and specify cryptographic options.

sections.title: Certificates and Named Options
sections.content:
The CERTS element carries a group of certificates as advisory data. The contents are not intended for display. The RFC permits certificate groups in PEM or PKCS-7 formats and says they can help a recipient obtain a certificate chain for a distinguished name in an anchor.

A CRYPTOPTS element can hold options under a name. An anchor can refer to that name using its CRYPTOPTS attribute; the name must begin with a number sign. Multiple CERTS elements are permitted, and the RFC suggests placing them in the document's HEAD element.
sections.plainLanguage: A page can include certificates for the recipient and can define a named set of cryptographic options. A link can refer to that named set.

sections.title: Example HTML Document
sections.content:
The example places a certificate group in a CERTS element with FMT=PKCS-7. An anchor then supplies a distinguished name and CRYPTOPTS values that describe S-HTTP privacy and signature-algorithm preferences.

The sample uses SGML quoting conventions to include quotation marks inside the distinguished name. Its anchor points to an S-HTTP URL.
sections.plainLanguage: The example puts certificate data in the document and places the recipient name and security settings on a link. The link uses an S-HTTP URL.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that the entire document is about security. It does not provide a separate list of security risks in its Security Considerations section.
sections.plainLanguage: This document describes security-related HTML syntax. Its security section offers no further risk analysis.

references.text: Rescorla, E. and A. Schiffman, "The Secure HyperText Transfer Protocol", RFC 2660, August 1999.
